title: Weak 'Soft Skills' Hurt Productivity, Employers Say
paragraphs: Technical knowledge is important in many jobs. But according to a new report, many employers in the UK are more worried about a shortage of basic "human" skills, such as communication, problem-solving and time management.

The report, called "Counting the Cost: The UK's Employability Skills Crisis," was published in September by City & Guilds, an organization that provides vocational training and qualifications. It surveyed 908 people who hire or manage staff, as well as 1,014 young people aged 18 to 24.

The study found that 38% of employers say a lack of these skills is holding back productivity and business growth. Employers reported a range of problems caused by these gaps, including mistakes and delays, higher staff turnover, reduced efficiency and weaker customer service. Meanwhile, 64% said it is becoming harder to find job applicants with these skills.
In fact, many employers now consider these skills more important than technical ability. Around 74% said employability skills matter more than technical knowledge for success at work.

The report also suggests that artificial intelligence may be making the problem worse. About 43% of employers use AI tools to screen job applicants, and 69% believe these tools rate technical ability more highly than the communication skills that companies say they need.

Young people have their own concerns. Around 51% said they fear AI will reduce job opportunities for their generation, and only 40% said they feel completely confident communicating face to face. Confidence was even lower among young people who are not in work, education or training. However, apprentices were more confident, with 48% saying they felt fully confident speaking to people in person.
Andy Moss, the interim chief executive of City & Guilds, argued that apprenticeships and other vocational routes help young people build these skills through real work.

The organization recommends that companies help workers develop these skills through onboarding programs, early career schemes and mentoring. It also suggests that companies review how their AI tools assess job candidates.
